en: 'Whoever opposes me, I, Esen,
Will bind him,' I used to say.
'Sparing none I meet,
I will kill them,' I used to say.
When I sent you to collect tribute,
You scattered all my possessions.
'I suffered humiliation from the Burut,' you said,
And fled back from Manas.
Witness my terrible wrath!
Though your name is champion Zholoy,
Rather than return fleeing from the Burut,
Sink into oblivion, as though never born!
Your khan who claims greatness—
Your courage is full, your fury strong,
Mighty Zholoy, my champion!
If you return without capturing Manas,
Give up all hope of your own life!
Achbuudan, the racer no bullet catches,
I will give you that chosen horse.
Though I fight single combats without cease,
Though I wage war seven years without pause,
I will give you a coat that never tears.
Their valor is extraordinary;
I will give you ten thousand Kytay troops.
That damned bloodstained one,
Unless you finally capture and bring him,
If Manas escapes alive,
Upon the whole world, slaughter
He seems ready to unleash.
Throwing the world into turmoil,
He seems ready to conquer it.
That damned Burut,
Capture him if you have the strength!
That raging Burut,
Kill him if he falls into your hands!
If Manas escapes, he will show no mercy;
He will certainly not leave us unharmed!
His armament numbers eighty-four.
That bloodstained one—may his house burn!—
If he lives and grows up,
Wherever he strikes will be red fire!
He is the lord, he is the khan;
Unless we catch him and prevent his escape,
He is the one who will crush us!
Unless we capture Manas,
Unless we put him in a deep pit,
I tremble before that bloodstained one.
'He will do what must not be done,' I say;
That is why I fear him.
If that bloodstained one returns,
He is the fierce one, he is the lion.
This very Beejin,
He is the warrior who will burn it down!
Dark hills, a high mountain—
No mountain to climb without looking.
That malicious bloodstained one
Is no enemy who will refrain from fighting!
He is the ruler, he is the lion.
That Burut—may he burn!—
Desired by his people, yet unknown to the nation,
Was born here in Altay.
If he lives, you will see:
He will raise an uproar in Beejin!
His father Jakyp and Akbaltay
Came to Altay driven into exile.
Wandering, unable to find a way,
Their hearts then blossomed and found peace.
Having come to Altay, that Jakyp
Raised countless livestock and grew wealthy.
Thinking him a Kalmyk, this Jakyp—
Cunning Jakyp seems to have hidden himself!
He himself follows Islam.
The forty households driven here
Seem to be enemies at heart.
Champions, I have sent you.
Unless you capture Manas,
Unless you put him in a deep pit,
Binding him so he cannot escape,
Unless you finish him off,
He is the place from which fire will spring;
He is the warrior accursed to burn!
All you champions, go!
My great royal marksman,
Karazhoy, you too must go!
The heroes Zholoy and great Döngö,
You have strength to match the world.
From sunrise to sunset,
You have steeds that can run the distance!
Tumult upon the world,
You have strength to unleash it!
You are champions, you are skilled;
Throwing the world into turmoil,
The whole world,
You are mighty enough to bind it.”
Esenkan pressed them harder:
“I give orders to the Kakan.
Not merely the Burut—I expect you,
The eighteen thousand worlds,
To bind them all and bring them here:
That is my wish!
Akbaltay and wealthy Jakyp,
'Your boy's name is Madman,' they said;
Cunning Jakyp kept him hidden.
Descend upon his head!
Scatter his four kinds of livestock!
Upon that mad wretch's house,
Enter grimly and force your way in.
Seize his scalp
And slit it a full handspan!
Say, 'Give us Manas!'
Return after forcing submission!
Use force against his champion;
Rush down in fury and surround him.
'The khan commands—hand him over!' say,
Scatter his ashes and beat him!
Bring his strong men bound.
Wealthy Jakyp and Akbaltay,
Kill them too!
Their swaggering khans,
Slaughter them as sacrifices!
Cut off their heads, bind them on,
And bring them toward us!
Their wrathful khans,
If they resist, knock the rage out of them!
Break their yurt roof crowns
And burn them in their own fires!
Give yourselves full rein.
If he looks to his livestock,
Strike his brains out and scatter them!
With that mad wretch, settle
The score from long ago!
That cunning Burut is treacherous.
Descend upon his head!
Fight him if you have the strength;
Scatter his four kinds of livestock!
Draw out his defiant words;
If that Burut strikes a sore spot,
Destroy and slaughter him!
Destroy many of them;
Slaughter them in a massacre!
Your khan, the hero Esenkan—
Do exactly as he says!
Slaughter their mighty men!”
Esenkan gave his terrible counsel:
“Now, champion, go!” he said.
“There in Baltay and Jakyp's land,
It seems a cunning ruler governs the people.
All who live there,
Kill them without leaving any alive,
Old Akbaltay and Jakyp too!”
“This is my command, champion,” he said.
When Esenkan issued his order,
Among the Kytay was Tagylyk;
The many officials swarmed.
The Kytay with rank buttons on their caps,
Their shaven-headed men gathered.
Their strong men grew excited:
Many champions, many giants,
Many mounted, many more on foot,
All champions, all giants,
The skilled among spearmen,
The excellent, full of resource,
Their heroes bearing battle-axes,
Their champions deft with spears,
Those who never retreated from death,
Those who never flinched a hair from doom.
When their khan gave the order,
They set out in a clamorous rush.
The eye could not pick them out;
No one could tell who was who.
The sky was clear, the earth overcast;
Not a speck of ground was visible.
Soil flew up and dust filled the land;
Not one person could be made out.
When Esenkan gave the order,
“Bloodstained Manas, the leopard,
Do not let him go—bring him bound!”
While their ruler spoke,
The iron-headed troops jostled;
They struggled with all their lives.
Their stone-badged men in short coats
Pressed against one another.
Charging in a noisy tumult,
They lost each other in the throng.
The eye could not pick them out;
May God never let you see it!
No one could tell who was who.
The Kytay were an orderly people,
Who had not been overwhelmed by the surging Deluge,
A people who had survived.
The accomplished champions made ready;
The seven divisions stirred.
Dust flew into the sky;
Champions marched in throngs.
Khan Zholoy of the Kalmyks,
His courage exceptional, his fury strong,
Leveled whoever attacked him.
If you see Zholoy, do not approach;
Abandon hope before this unbeliever!
They clothed him in blue armor
And mounted him on Achbuudan.
Broad of girth, short of stature,
Round-faced, broad-shouldered,
Sparing none who grappled with him,
With the meat of a whole young bull,
He was not sated at a single meal.
His prowess was extraordinary;
His valor was considerable.
Wrapped in blue armor,
If you saw great Zholoy,
Raging like a gray boar,
Smoke billowing from his mouth,
Flame streaming from his eyes—
Such was that mad wretch.
His champions of many kinds,
He took his army in full.
Not merely Manas—that mad wretch
Had power to match the world!
His mace was half a mountain's size.
Do not ask about Zholoy:
He seemed ready to devour anyone he saw.
The finest among champions,
If you ask about Zholoy,
He was a lord of the black Kalmyks.
Born in the west,
An outstanding champion, a great glutton,
He killed those who attacked
And raised an uproar among humankind.
The finest among those with gray yurt coverings,
Such was Zholoy:
A lord of the black Kalmyks,
The summit of a snowy mountain,
A prince of the black Kalmyks.
Zholoy took the road
With an army numbering one thousand.
The one he would bind was wealthy Jakyp;
The one he would fight was Akbaltay;
The one he would grapple with was Khan Manas.
If these fell into his hands,
If his strength and power sufficed,
He would gouge out their eyes in torment.
Manas and the Kyrgyz forty households—
He would drink their blood until sated.
Behind that Zholoy,
Clad in bright red finery,
One held precious in Beejin,
Whose fame was heard and known,
Whose prowess was extraordinary,
Whose valor was considerable,
Whose very name inspired fear,
A skilled horseman, swift on foot,
Learned in wondrous arts,
A powerful sorcerer, a great weather-conjurer,
Came before the khan.
One who came forth when trouble broke,
An expert, valiant marksman,
